name: Common mistakes and false friends
intro: The grammar mistakes Norwegian learners make most often – subject–verb agreement, much/many, it/there, the article – and false friends between Norwegian and English.
sammendrag:
## Learning from mistakes

Norwegian and English are closely related, which makes English easier to learn. But the similarities also cause typical mistakes, because we are tempted to translate directly. Knowing the most common traps helps you avoid them.

## Subject–verb agreement

The verb must agree with the subject. In the present simple, **he, she and it** need **-s**: She **plays**, it **works**. With **there is / there are**, the verb agrees with what comes after: There **is** a problem. There **are** two problems. Words like **everybody**, **nobody** and **each** are singular: Everybody **is** here. **People** and **police** are plural: The police **are** coming.

## Much or many?

**Many** is used with things we can count: many books, many people. **Much** is used with things we cannot count: much water, much time. The same goes for **few/little** and **fewer/less**. Some nouns are uncountable in English but countable in Norwegian: **information**, **advice**, **furniture**, **news**, **homework**. We say “a piece of advice”, not “an advice”, and “The news **is** good”.

## It or there?

Norwegian “det” can be both **it** and **there** in English. Use **there** when something exists or is present: **There is** a cat in the garden. Use **it** about something already mentioned, or about weather and time: **It is** raining. **It is** late.

## Articles

English uses **a/an** with jobs: She is **a** doctor. English usually does **not** use the article with general ideas, meals and many institutions: **Life** is short. We had **dinner**. He is in **hospital** (British).

## Adjective or adverb?

Use an **adjective** to describe a noun and an **adverb** to describe a verb: She is a **good** singer. She sings **well**. He drives **carefully**, not “careful”.

## False friends

**False friends** look similar to Norwegian words but mean something else:

- **eventually** = til slutt (not eventuelt – that is “possibly”)
- **actually** = faktisk (not aktuelt – that is “relevant”)
- **sensible** = fornuftig (not sensibel – that is “sensitive”)
- **fabric** = stoff (not fabrikk – that is “factory”)
- **become** = bli (not bekomme)
- **brave** = modig (not brav – that is “well-behaved”)

## Tip

Make your own list of mistakes you often make, and check your texts for them before you hand them in.

flashcards.def: The verb must match the subject: she plays, they play.
The verb agrees with what follows: there is a cat, there are two cats.
Everybody, nobody and each are singular.
Police and people are plural in English.
With countable nouns: many books, many people.
With uncountable nouns: much water, much time.
information, advice, furniture, news, homework – no plural and no “a”.
There = something exists. It = something already mentioned, weather, time.
Adjective and adverb: a good singer, she sings well.

quiz.explain: With “she” in the present simple, the verb needs -s: she plays.

quiz.text: Choose the correct word: “There … two cars outside.”
quiz.explain: The verb agrees with “two cars”, which is plural: there are.

quiz.text: Choose the correct word: “How … money do you have?”
quiz.explain: Money is uncountable, so we use “much”.

options: Can you give me an advice?
Can you give me two advice?
Can you give me some advices?
Can you give me some advice?
quiz.explain: “Advice” is uncountable in English. Say “some advice” or “a piece of advice”.

quiz.text: Choose the correct word: “… is raining again.”
quiz.explain: We use “it” about the weather: It is raining.
English uses a/an before jobs: She is a doctor.

quiz.text: Choose the correct word: “He drives very …”
quiz.explain: An adverb describes how he drives: carefully.
“Sensible” means “fornuftig”. “Sensibel” in Norwegian is “sensitive” in English.
“Everybody” is grammatically singular: Everybody is here.

ekstra.text: “The news are good” is correct English.
ekstra.explain: “News” is uncountable and singular: The news is good.
“Actually” is a false friend. “Aktuelt” is “relevant” or “current”.

ekstra.text: “Many” is used with uncountable nouns like water.
ekstra.explain: “Many” is for countable nouns. With water we use “much”.

ekstra.text: “There is a cat in the garden” uses “there” because the sentence says that something exists.
ekstra.explain: “There is/are” introduces something that exists or is present.
“Fabric” is cloth or material. A factory is “fabrikk”.

ekstra.text: Choose the correct word: “There were … people at the concert than last year.”

ekstra.explain: “Well” is the adverb that describes how she sings.

skriv.text: Norwegian and English are closely related, which can make English easier to learn. Why can this similarity also lead to mistakes?
skriv.fasit: Because the languages are similar, learners may translate directly from Norwegian. A direct translation can lead to typical mistakes in English.
kriterier: Explains that the languages’ similarity can tempt learners to translate directly.
Connects direct translation with making mistakes in English.

skriv.text: Complete the sentences and explain why the verbs are different: “Everybody ___ ready, but the police ___ coming.”
skriv.fasit: Everybody is ready, but the police are coming. Everybody is singular, while police is plural in English.
kriterier: Uses “is” with “everybody” because it is singular.
Uses “are” with “police” because it is plural in English.

skriv.text: Correct this sentence and explain the noun mistake: “I got an advice and two informations.”
skriv.fasit: I got a piece of advice and some information. “Advice” and “information” are uncountable nouns in English, so they do not take “a” or a plural ending.
kriterier: Correctly uses “a piece of advice” or another correct form without “an advice”.
Uses “information” without a plural ending and recognises that it is uncountable.

skriv.text: Correct both sentences and explain the article use: “She is doctor. We had a dinner.”
skriv.fasit: She is a doctor. We had dinner. English uses “a” with jobs but usually no article with meals.
kriterier: Removes “a” before “dinner” and explains that meals usually have no article.

skriv.text: A learner writes, “Actually, I might visit if I have time,” but means “possibly.” Explain what is wrong and replace “Actually” with the right word.
skriv.fasit: “Actually” means “faktisk,” not “possibly.” The learner should write, “Possibly, I might visit if I have time.”
kriterier: Replaces “Actually” with “Possibly” or another suitable way to express “possibly”.

skriv.text: A learner means they work in a factory but writes, “I work in a fabric.” Correct the sentence and explain the difference between “fabric” and “factory.”
skriv.fasit: The correct sentence is, “I work in a factory.” “Fabric” means “stoff,” while “factory” means “fabrikk.”
kriterier: Distinguishes the meanings: fabric is stoff and factory is fabrikk.

skriv.text: A Norwegian speaker thinks the English word “brave” means “brav.” Explain the mistake and say what “brave” means in English.
skriv.fasit: “Brave” does not mean “brav”; it means “modig.” The similar-looking words have different meanings.
kriterier: Explains that it does not mean Norwegian “brav” (well-behaved).

skriv.text: You have already introduced a cat by writing, “There is a cat in the garden.” Write a sentence saying that the cat is black, and explain why it starts with “it” or “there.”
skriv.fasit: It is black. Use “it” because the cat has already been mentioned.
kriterier: Begins the sentence with “It” and says the cat is black.
Explains that “it” refers to something already mentioned.
